common_name: Gatsby Star Oakleaf Hydrangea (Double-Flowered White Panicle Oakleaf Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Gatsby Star is part of the Gatsby series bred for improved flower form and vigor over older oakleaf hydrangea cultivars.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade. Gatsby Star bears large, upright flower panicles made up of unusually showy double florets, each outer flower resembling a small starry rosette rather than the simple four-petaled florets typical of most oakleaf hydrangea, giving the whole panicle a fuller, more textured look that ages from white to a soft pink-tan. Bold, deeply lobed leaves turn brilliant orange-red-purple in fall on a vigorous, well-branched plant, and exfoliating cinnamon-colored bark adds winter structure after leaf drop. As with other oakleaf hydrangeas, flower buds form on old wood, so prune only in the weeks immediately following bloom to avoid removing the next season's flowers.

common_name: Bristol Ruby Weigela (Classic Ruby-Red Flowered Weigela)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Bristol Ruby is a long-cultivated mid-20th-century weigela cultivar still widely grown for its reliable, saturated flower color.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Bristol Ruby is a classic, long-cultivated weigela producing abundant clusters of deep ruby-red, trumpet-shaped flowers in a heavy late-spring flush that hummingbirds visit reliably. It grows into a larger, more traditional upright-arching shrub than the many compact modern weigela cultivars, useful as an informal hedge, background shrub, or specimen where more size is wanted. It tolerates heat and average garden soil well and is generally trouble-free, needing only a light shaping prune right after flowering, since it blooms on the previous year's wood and pruning at other times removes the coming season's flowers.

common_name: Eva Rathke Weigela (Historic Dark Red Weigela)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Eva Rathke is one of the oldest named weigela cultivars still in cultivation, dating to the late 1800s.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Eva Rathke is one of the oldest weigela cultivars still commonly grown, dating to the late 1800s and prized for dark crimson-red, trumpet-shaped flowers held in dense clusters through a heavy late-spring bloom flush. Its long garden history and reliable performance have kept it in cultivation for well over a century, and its color remains among the deepest reds available in the genus. It tolerates heat and average garden soil well; prune only right after flowering to shape the plant, since weigela blooms on the previous year's wood and later pruning sacrifices the next season's flowers.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Java Red foliage color develops best with at least six hours of direct sun.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Java Red bears bronze-purple foliage that holds its color through the growing season, providing months of interest beyond its clusters of pale pink, trumpet-shaped spring flowers, which stand out clearly against the dark leaves. Its moderate, well-rounded size fits mixed borders and foundation plantings without the size management larger species weigela can need. It is generally tough and trouble-free, tolerating heat and average garden soil well, and needs only a light shaping prune right after flowering, since weigela sets next year's flower buds on the current season's wood soon after bloom ends.
